Abstract—The construction of new type of power system 
with an increasing integration of renewable energy generation 
has become the mainstream trend in current power system 
development. The rising penetration of renewable energy poses 
challenges to the stability of the power system, making it 
increasingly important to assess renewable energy hosting 
capacity while considering system stability constraints.  This 
paper establishes a method for assessing renewable energy 
hosting capacity considering static voltage stabil ity. Firstly, it 
reviews and analyzes commonly used static voltage stability 
indices in power systems, selecting the L -index for detailed 
modeling. Building upon this, a renewable energy hosting 
capacity assessment model incorporating the L-index is 
developed, and a solution strategy based on the primal -dual 
interior point method is proposed. Subsequently, the study 
analyzes the impact of considering static voltage stability on the 
assessment results of renewable energy hosting  capacity using 
an enhanced IEEE 30-bus test case. 
Keywords—r enewable energy, hosting capacity assessment , 
static voltage stability, L-index. 
I. INTRODUCTION  
As early as the 1940s, Marković raised concerns about 
voltage stability in power systems. With the continuous 
expansion of power grid scale and increasing penetration of 
renewable energy, the industry has placed greater emphasis on 
voltage stability issues. In recent years, large -scale system 
incidents caused by renewable energy in modern power 
systems have also become more frequent. 
The dynamic equations of power systems can be 
succinctly described as a complex set of nonlinear equations. 
Specifically, they can be represented by a set of nonlinear 
differential-difference-algebraic equations (DDAEs), which 
form the foundation for addressing all voltage stability issues 
in power systems
[1].  
Static voltage instability occurs when the voltage level of 
a power system gradually decreases as the load increases. This 
instability reaches a critical state when the load grows to a 
point where the system can no longer support it. Static voltage 
stability involves identifying a time -domain section of the 
power system's dynamic processes. Mathematically, in 
DDAEs, this can be simplified by fixing the difference 
equations in the DDAE and approximating the differentiation 
of state variables to zero.
 [5]This transformation allows the 
DDAE system to be described purely by algebraic equations. 
Following this logic, static voltage stability is solely 
related to the algebraic equations describing the system. 
Analytical methods for assessing static voltage stability can 
generally be categorized into two approaches: static voltage 
stability indices
 [6][7]and methods such as the continuation 
power flow or direct methods  [8][9]based on continuous flow 
analysis. Common assessment indices for static voltage 
stability margin include sensitivity index[10][11], eigenvalue and 
singular value indices[12][13], singular value indices[14], margin 
indices [15], V/V0 index [16], voltage stability proximity index, 
etc. The static voltage stability L index (L index), proposed by 
Kessel in 1986, belongs to the category of voltage stability 
proximity indices
[17]. The L index is based on power flow 
solutions and is defined through the derivation of system 
network equations. It is a stability index that intuitively 
reflects the distance between the current operating state of the 
system and static voltage collapse. Due to its early proposal, 
the L index has been widely applied in the analysis of static 
voltage stability in power systems and exhibits strong 
accuracy. Given the excellent performance of the L index in 
assessing static voltage stability, this section will employ the 
L index to evaluate the static voltage stability of the system. 
The subsequent section will provide a theoretical basis by 
detailing the establishment and derivation process of the L 
index, supporting the assessment of renewable energy 
integration considering static voltage stability.

B. Comparison 
1) Consideration of the L -index Absorption Model and 
Traditional Absorption Model 
Based on the mathematical model established earlier, set 
up control groups for the traditional absorption model and the 
L-index absorption model. In Scenario 1, the L -index 
absorption model considers the same mathematical setup as 
earlier, with a static voltage stability L-index constraint where 
Lmax=0.4. In Scenario 2, the traditional absorption model 
does not consider the static voltage stability L-index constraint, 
omitting equations (7) and (8) from the previously established 
model. The absorption resul ts of the two scenarios are 
analyzed as follows: 
a) Static Voltage Stability 
After evaluating the L-index in the absorption models, it is 
observed that the overall L -index in the L -index absorption 
model is generally lower compared to the traditional 
absorption model. Additionally, the peak L -index in the L -
index absorption model evaluation is 0.3982 p.u., significantly 
lower than the peak L -index of 0.4417 p.u. in the traditional 
absorption model. This demonstrates that the absorption 
model considering the L -index can achieve better static 
voltage stability. The calculated average voltage in the L -
index absorption model is 0.9983 p.u., whereas in the 
traditional absorption model, it is 0.9935 p.u., further 
supporting the superior static voltage stability of the L-index 
absorption model.

After considering the assessment model of the L index for 
calculation and analysis, it is found that when renewable

voltage stability, the absorption capacity of renewable energy 
will be significantly reduced. 
V. S
UMMARY 
This article first studies the static voltage stability 
indicators and related analysis and calculation methods of the 
power system. The L indicator is selected to evaluate the static 
voltage stability of the studied system. Subsequently, based on 
the static voltage stability L index, a renewable energy hosting 
capacity assessment model considering the L index was 
established. By comparing the evaluation results of the 
system's absorption capacity under different L
max settings, it 
was found that the evaluat ion results of the system's 
absorption capacity were basically positively correlated with 
the value of L
max, that is, the larger the L max value, the better 
the evaluation results of the system's absorption capacity. The 
conclusion can be achieved that when renewable energy units 
are connected to nodes with higher L index, the system's 
absorption rate and amount are higher. This conclusion can 
have certain reference value for renewable energy site 
selection.
